segments.text: Please welcome to the stage the founder of Black Hat, Jeff Moss.
Hello. Hey, thank you for coming to our afternoon keynote session.
Main stage, we like to call it for the afternoon. And I'm going to be
introducing Chris Inglis. I've known Chris for a while.
Kind of, he doesn't know what I'm going to say, so I'm going to surprise
him with this. But we talked a bit after the Snowden leaks when he was
the number two at NSA, and unfortunately he had to deal a lot with that
situation. And I remember some of the advice I gave him back then was the
information is just going to drip and drip and drip. And unless you can somehow
get out ahead of it, it's just going to consume the news cycle forever.
And it really feels like that was a glimpse into our future, because if you
look at how algorithmic or non-algorithmically generated campaigns are,
they're designed to consume the news cycle and drip and drip and drip.
So Chris has spent essentially his whole professional career in service to the country After
NSA, he became the nation's first director of ONCD, Office of the National Cyber Director,
moving from intelligence to the White House, from DOD to the White House, where he
was tasked with really setting up that office from scratch. And
since leaving government, he stayed really engaged. And so one of the reasons why I
really enjoy talking to Chris is I just I just like listening to him talk.
His word selection, the way his perspective, the way he's so articulate,
I just really find his perspective refreshing and thoughtful. And so I'm hoping,
as I sit in the audience with you, I'm really looking forward to seeing how
some of his views have changed now being in civilian life and reflecting back
on some of his past So, anyway, if anybody could please give me a warm
round of applause for Chris Inglis.
Hey, good afternoon, and thanks for coming to the Coveted After Lunch spot. And Jeff,
thank you so much for that warm welcome. I remember that conversation, too. I only
wish we'd had it in 2012. So, I'm going to actually tell some stories
today. That's usually the way I speak. But along the way, what I'm going to
try to do is develop a model, a model that is forward-looking about how we
should think about this realm known as cyberspace and what we should do about it.
And that model will then, having been placed in a forward position, not benefit terribly
much from generative AI. So I'm going to disappoint you by not talking a lot
about that, but rather through human agency and aspiration. The title of the talk that
I originally proposed was Security in the Age of Cyber, but I changed my mind
because I think that when we say cyber, or worse, when we say cyber security,
people immediately outside of this audience, outside of Black Hat say, thank God it's not
about me. They think that this is about something else that the IT specialist or
the cyber specialist are going to work and take off my plate. And then they
realize that we're all implicated in this. Later I'll use this again, but I love
one of the questions that Jeff asked in many of his talks, which is why
do race cars have bigger brakes? So they can go faster. It's not about the
brakes, it's about the car. It's about the performance of the thing you already care

some skilling. And so I think this might be a more appropriate title. How do
we get cyberspace to meet our needs? How do we get digital infrastructure to meet
our needs? And frankly, just about everything I'm going to tell you today, I learned
from you. I learned from all the people that I've had the pleasure, the privilege
of associating with over a now 50 year plus career in public service.
And from leaders that have taught me many things, not least of which how to
lead. From Dorothy Denning and Sheila Brand back 50 years ago,
to Jenny Easterly and Jeff Moss more recently, and everyone in between. Part of my
message is thank you for helping me come to some of these conclusions, which I
use to guide my contributions to the various things that I do. I'm gonna start
here. When I showed up at the US Air Force Academy in 1972, I know
it was a long time ago, but they had airplanes even then, I received my
first computer as they do today, and this was it. It was a slide roll,
and this one still works. Unlike most computers that you might have received as your
first computer. Of course, I don't know how to work it, but it works. And
what's extraordinary about this is that this was at the center of the computing world

years. From 1620 to 1972, this was the dominant computer used. We built the
Boeing 747 with this. We built the Empire State Building with this. We did the

35s using reverse polis notation, some of you may know where I am on that,

As in the same course. It's been ever thus that technology can enable the human
being in the same way that generative AI does that to do. But this is
where I started. I'm gonna put this over here because that's gonna be my point
of departure. Because what I'm gonna do is to essentially do a brief reprise of
what happened in the last 50 years. Not because I'm maudlin or affectionate about the
last 50 years. I think it's really important to understand what developed how, what we
did about it, what we didn't, to know what we actually are sitting on top
of today. As you all know, kind of beginning in the 1970s, We began to
develop ever more powerful processors and data centers might have been contained in the

doubled and doubled again every year, year and a half or so. And it began
to look increasingly like this. At the same time, we developed the communications, the bandwidth,

along. Then we built this logic layer between them that would essentially create some
degree of rules, protocols, coherence, so that this system could operate not as a

interesting about this is we began then to defer to the logic of this logic

representation in this space. And then we said, Oh, what the heck, let's just store
our bank accounts in this space. So bank accounts became ones and zeros secrets became
ones and zeros and they began to be permanently stored in this space. We began

miracle of the internet that shouldn't surprise any of you. But It turns out that
those were always developed in the context of these two layers. You've got this people
layer called the persona layer at the top, and you've got this geographic layer at

when you're all done, kind of now, is a cyberspace that really looks like this
and behaves like this. It's a vertical kind of thing. which is that any one
of those people using any one of those devices, relying on that logic layer, using

And any action taken in that space actually takes some influence or is affected by

defend something in this space typically happens horizontally in this space. We come up with

perhaps some bandwidth or something stored out in the cloud. Very seldom do I see

pieces, you have to actually consider what's gonna happen to all the other pieces. You

of those. One of my messages going forward is we have to account for all

going to use as I build my model forward. Cyberspace is the sum of technology

me introduce the concept of models because what I'm gonna do from this forward is

two words? Two words, not good, right? Now, I say that not simply because there's

At any moment in time, we've got a good kind of situation or a bad

right? We were able to generate a vaccine in 18 months in the onset of

I would offer that the difference between those is not fate. It's not gonna be

But we will be a little bit lower and a little bit slower. moment goes

when you lose an engine, kind of no matter how many you have, you are

I said, what's the second thing? So the second thing is, it's our home. It

must leverage all instruments of power in that collective defense. There's nothing kind of ambiguous
